summary: John the Baptist tells Jerusalem’s envoys he is only a voice, then points to Jesus: the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin, the Son of God.
key_insight: John was born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1:36), yet he says of Him, “He was before me.” The Baptist is not speaking of age. He is pointing past the Man from Nazareth to the Word who “was in the beginning with God” (John 1:2).
story: While John was baptizing at Bethabara beyond the Jordan, the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?” He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, “I am not the Christ.”

“What then? Are you Elijah?” they asked. He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” He answered, “No.” They pressed him for something to take back to those who sent them: “What do you say about yourself?” John answered in the words of the prophet Isaiah. He was “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” calling, “Make straight the way of the LORD.”

The men who had been sent were from the Pharisees, and they wanted to know by what right he acted: “Why then do you baptize if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?” John said, “I baptize with water, but there stands One among you whom you do not know.” This One was coming after him, yet was preferred before him, and John was not worthy to loose His sandal strap.

The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world! This is He of whom I said, ‘After me comes a Man who is preferred before me, for He was before me.’ ”

“I did not know Him,” John said, but he had come baptizing with water so that this Man “should be revealed to Israel.” Then John bore witness to what he had seen: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and He remained upon Him.”

God, who had sent John to baptize, had given him a sign beforehand: the one on whom he saw the Spirit descending and remaining would be the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. John had seen it happen. “And I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.”

fit.question: John told the delegation plainly that he was not Elijah (John 1:21). Yet Jesus said of him, “he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14). Did John contradict Jesus?

points.label: The question they asked
points.text: Malachi had promised that God would send “Elijah the prophet” before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Many took this to mean that Elijah himself, carried to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11), would come back in person. Asked whether he was that man, John told the truth: he was not.

points.label: The calling Jesus meant
points.text: Before John was born, the angel told Zacharias that his son would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). Jesus spoke of that calling, and He added, “if you are willing to receive it,” a sign that He was not speaking of Elijah in person. Later He said Elijah had come already, and the disciples understood that He meant John (Matthew 17:12–13).

fit.note: John denied a mistaken identity, and Jesus affirmed a real calling. Both statements are true at once.
fit.short: John denied being Elijah come back in person; Jesus meant that John filled Elijah’s role, “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17).

fit.question: Twice John says, “I did not know Him” (John 1:31, 33). Yet in Matthew, when Jesus came to be baptized, John protested, “I need to be baptized by You” (Matthew 3:14). How could he protest if he did not know Him?

points.label: Known as a man, not yet as the One
points.text: John and Jesus were relatives (Luke 1:36), but John grew up in the wilderness (Luke 1:80) and Jesus in Nazareth. What John knew of Jesus was enough to make him feel unworthy. What he did not yet have was God’s own word that this was the Coming One. As McGarvey put it, John believed it before he knew it.

points.label: A witness waits for the sign
points.text: God had told John what to watch for: the Spirit descending and remaining on one man (John 1:33). John’s task was to testify, and a witness speaks of what he has seen. His protest came before the baptism; the sign came with it; his public testimony came after it.

fit.note: John’s reverence came first, and God’s sign turned it into testimony. The two accounts describe stages in one man’s knowing, not a contradiction.
fit.short: John knew Jesus well enough to feel unworthy, but he did not know Him as the Messiah until God’s sign, the Spirit remaining on Him.

scene.label: Priests and Levites
scene.text: John’s Gospel often uses “the Jews” for the religious leaders in Jerusalem. They sent men from the temple: priests, who served at the altar and judged matters of cleansing, and Levites, who assisted them and taught the law (Nehemiah 8:7–9). A prophet washing crowds in the Jordan was their concern. John himself was the son of a priest, Zacharias (Luke 1:5).

scene.label: Elijah and the Prophet
scene.text: The Old Testament closes with God’s promise to send Elijah before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5–6). Moses had promised that God would raise up “a Prophet like me” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Some in Jesus’ day thought of the Prophet as someone other than the Christ (John 7:40–41), so the delegation asked about each in turn.

scene.label: Bethabara beyond the Jordan
scene.text: “Beyond the Jordan” means the east bank, probably in Perea. Most Greek manuscripts, including the oldest, call the place Bethany, a different village from the Bethany near Jerusalem. The exact site is unknown: tradition points to a crossing near Jericho, while others look farther north. Jesus later returned to “the place where John was baptizing at first” (John 10:40).

scene.label: The sin of the world
scene.text: John says “sin,” singular: the whole weight of guilt, and not Israel’s alone but the world’s. The sacrifices of the law could not take sin away (Hebrews 10:4). Isaiah’s Servant would do what they could not: “He bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12).

scene.label: Baptism with the Holy Spirit
scene.text: The prophets promised a day when God would put His Spirit within His people (Ezekiel 36:27; Joel 2:28). John could wash only with water. The One on whom the Spirit remained would pour the Spirit out on others, as Jesus did at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:33).

witnesses.john: John alone records this questioning and this testimony. His Gospel does not describe the baptism; it gives the witness of the man who saw it, framed by “this is the testimony of John” (1:19) and “I have seen and testified” (1:34). The first words spoken about Jesus as He steps into John’s story are “Behold! The Lamb of God,” and the same Gospel shows Him dying at Passover with not one bone broken (19:36).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Lamb who carries away the sin of the world, and the eternal Son who was before John though born after him. The Spirit remains on Him, and He gives that Spirit to others.
seeing.living: When John sees Jesus, his first word is “Behold!”: look at Him. John’s baptism could call people to confess their sin; only the Lamb could take it away. Bring your guilt to Jesus instead of trying to wash it off yourself, and then speak of Him as John did, from what you have seen.
seeing.ponder: When the weight of your sin presses on you, where do you look: at yourself, or at the Lamb of God who takes it away?

preaching.big_idea: John was only a voice, so that every eye would turn to the Lamb of God.
outline: The Lamb who takes away sin (29–31)
The Son on whom the Spirit remains (32–34)
preaching.watch_for: The passage is framed by testimony: “this is the testimony of John” (19) and “I have seen and testified” (34). Twice John says, “I did not know Him” (31, 33). His witness rests on God’s sign, not on family ties.
